title: Surprise Ministry Audit
description: Two auditors from the ministry appear at your door, unannounced. They want to see documentation.

options.label: Drop everything and assist
options.outcome: You spend the day pulling files and answering questions. They seem satisfied.

options.label: Ask to reschedule
options.outcome: They confer in the parking lot and agree to come back next week. You have time to prepare, or to worry.
options.failureOutcome: They decline, politely, and set up in your boardroom anyway. The audit proceeds today with a note already made that the licensee asked them to leave.

options.label: Delegate to your team
options.outcome: Karen handles it. She finds a few gaps before they do and smooths them over.
options.partialOutcome: Karen gets through the day, but the auditors note the manager was unavailable. One of the gaps becomes a written observation instead of a conversation.
options.failureOutcome: Karen fumbles a question about referral sign-off and the room goes quiet. The gaps become a formal finding, and a follow-up visit is scheduled with the tone already set.

title: Audit Follow-up Visit
description: The auditors return. They want updated referral notes, professional sign-off, and evidence you addressed the last gaps.

options.label: Present a remediation package
options.outcome: You hand over a clean package with clear corrective actions. The tone softens.

options.label: Ask for more time (again)
options.outcome: They grant a short extension and note the pattern. You buy a little time at the cost of some credibility.
options.failureOutcome: Refused. Findings are issued on the spot, with the delay pattern cited in them, and you are now remediating under a formal order instead of a conversation.

options.label: Throw the team under the bus
options.outcome: The deflection lands, for now. The auditors write up a staffing issue, and the office hears exactly how it was framed.
options.failureOutcome: They interview the team directly and the stories do not line up with yours. The finding stands, the office knows what you tried, and the auditors now treat everything you say as management spin.

title: Audit Findings Released
description: Last quarter's audit results are in. There are "concerns" about referral documentation.

options.label: Accept findings and remediate
options.outcome: You allocate budget to fix the gaps. It's the mature response.

options.label: Request reconsideration
options.outcome: You push back respectfully with documentation. Some findings are reduced, though the relationship cools a degree.
options.failureOutcome: The findings are upheld in full and your file gains a note about a combative response. The next audit will open from that note, and you still owe the remediation.

options.label: Blame the previous administration
options.outcome: Classic move. It works politically, and colleagues quietly file it away.
options.failureOutcome: Someone produces a memo with your signature on the referral process in question. The deflection becomes its own story, and you remediate the findings anyway with your credibility spent.

title: Angry Stakeholder Call
description: The Chief of a partner Nation is on the line. They're not happy about something in Block 7.

options.label: Listen and apologize
options.outcome: You hear them out. By the end, tensions have eased. A site visit is promised.

options.label: Explain the regulatory constraints
options.outcome: You walk through the rules. They understand the framework but feel dismissed by it.
options.failureOutcome: They hear a lecture, not an answer, and end the call early. By Friday the Nation has taken Block 7 over your head to the district, and the file pauses while the ministry asks you to explain the same rules to them.

options.label: Offer to halt operations pending review
options.outcome: A dramatic gesture. It costs production but rebuilds trust.

title: Community Complaint
description: A petition from the local community lands on your desk. Concerns about truck traffic.

options.label: Schedule a town hall meeting
options.outcome: You set up an evening session. Good turnout, reasonable discussion, and the petition organizers leave with your phone number instead of a grievance.
options.partialOutcome: The room is thin and the questions are sharp. You hold the line but commit to a written follow-up on two points you could not answer, and the petition stays open.
options.failureOutcome: The meeting turns hostile twenty minutes in, with a reporter taking notes in the back row. The petition becomes an organized campaign with a mailing list, and your next haul schedule will be written with them in mind.

options.label: Send a written response
options.outcome: A detailed letter explaining safety measures. Polite but distant.

options.label: Redirect to the ministry
options.outcome: You forward it to the proper authority. Not your problem now.

title: Media Inquiry
description: A reporter is asking questions about your latest timber sale. Tone seems skeptical.

options.label: Give a full interview
options.outcome: You spend an hour explaining the complexities. The story runs balanced, and the reporter keeps your number for next time.
options.partialOutcome: The story is mostly fair but leads with your one clumsy quote. You spend the next morning on calls making sure the ministry read past the headline.
options.failureOutcome: An hour of tape becomes a skeptical piece with your two worst sentences in it. The ministry calls before you have read it, and the next story about this sale will start from the frame this one set.

options.label: Provide a written statement only
options.outcome: Controlled messaging. The story runs with minimal quotes.

options.label: Decline to comment
options.outcome: "Company declined to comment." Never looks great.

title: System Crash
description: The permit tracking database just went down. IT is "looking into it."

options.label: Switch to paper backup
options.outcome: Old school but functional. Productivity drops but work continues.

options.label: Send everyone home early
options.outcome: Nothing can be done without the system. Team appreciates the break.

options.label: Escalate to management
options.outcome: You make noise. IT reprioritizes your fix and the system is back by mid-afternoon, half a day gone.
options.failureOutcome: The noise gets you a ticket number and nothing else. The day is lost anyway, the team switches to paper at 3 p.m., and management remembers who called twice about a database.

title: GIS Data Corrupted
description: The spatial files for three pending permits are corrupted. Backups are weeks old.

options.label: Rebuild from field notes
options.outcome: Painful work but you reconstruct the data. Lost two days.

options.label: Request extension from ministry
options.outcome: They grant two weeks and note the delay in your file. The rebuild happens on a survivable schedule.
options.failureOutcome: Refused — the deadline stands. You submit what you have with no time to check it, review flags the stale layers, and the resubmission now happens on the reviewer's schedule instead of yours.

options.label: Submit with old data and notes
options.outcome: The package clears review with the vintage of the spatial data noted and nothing more said. You got away with it, and the file says so quietly.
options.partialOutcome: It goes through, conditionally. The reviewer flags the data vintage and requires corrected spatial within thirty days, and your submissions now get opened carefully instead of stamped.
options.failureOutcome: Rejected outright, with the stale data called out by name. You are rebuilding from field notes anyway — now with a compliance mark attached and a reviewer who reads everything your office sends.

title: Budget Cut Announced
description: Finance just announced a 15% reduction to your operating budget. Effective immediately.

options.label: Accept and adjust plans
options.outcome: You revise the work plan. Some projects will wait.

options.label: Fight for restoration
options.outcome: You make the case upstairs with numbers and a straight face. Partial restoration is granted, at a price in favours.
options.failureOutcome: Nothing comes back. The full cut stands, the favours are spent, and you are now revising the same work plan you refused to trim two weeks ago — remembered upstairs as the manager who fought it.

options.label: Find alternative funding
options.outcome: You scramble for grants and partner contributions. Most of the gap gets covered, stressfully.
options.failureOutcome: Weeks of applications and calls land nothing. The shortfall comes out of the work plan after all, a month later than if you had just cut it, and the backlog grew while you wrote proposals.

title: Policy Change
description: New guidelines just dropped. Your current permits need additional documentation.

options.label: Comply immediately
options.outcome: Extra paperwork slows the file, but you stay ahead of enforcement.

options.label: Request grandfathering
options.outcome: Existing permits are exempted. New files still need the extra documentation, but the backlog stays manageable.
options.failureOutcome: Refused — and the request itself flags your existing permits for a closer read under the new rules. You are now re-documenting files that were closed, on the district's timeline.

options.label: Join industry pushback
options.outcome: You sign onto the letter. Implementation is delayed a quarter, which is all anyone really wanted.
options.failureOutcome: The pushback fails and the signatory list circulates at the district. The rules land on schedule, your files start moving slower than everyone else's, and you get to comply anyway — late.

title: Leadership Shuffle
description: Your ministry contact just got transferred. The replacement starts next month.

options.label: Rush pending items through
options.outcome: Your contact signs off on the pending items in her last two weeks. Approvals in hand before the desk changes.
options.failureOutcome: The rush is visible from across the office. Two files bounce for haste, the outgoing contact stops returning calls, and the replacement inherits a sticky note about your district — you resubmit to someone you have already annoyed.

options.label: Prepare a transition briefing
options.outcome: Good relationship management. The new contact appreciates the context.

options.label: Wait and see
options.outcome: Things slow down during the transition. Expected.

title: Team Conflict
description: Two of your team members had a heated argument in the break room. Tensions are high.

options.label: Mediate directly
options.outcome: You sit them down together. Issues get aired, a working truce holds, and the break room is usable again.
options.failureOutcome: The session blows up inside ten minutes. One of them requests a transfer by email that afternoon, the office starts picking sides, and HR is now involved on their terms instead of yours.

options.label: Assign them to separate projects
options.outcome: Physical distance helps. Underlying issue remains.

options.label: Bring in HR
options.outcome: Formal process begins. Professional but cold.

title: Resignation Notice
description: Your most experienced analyst just gave two weeks notice. Better opportunity.

options.label: Counter-offer with raise
options.outcome: They think it over the weekend and stay. Continuity preserved, budget dented.
options.partialOutcome: They stay, and the team now knows exactly what a resignation letter is worth. Two more calendar invites titled career discussion appear within the month.
options.failureOutcome: Your counter becomes their leverage at the other shop, and they leave anyway with a better title. The handover is two distracted weeks, and fifteen years of file knowledge walks out the door.

options.label: Wish them well and plan transition
options.outcome: Professional departure. Knowledge transfer happens. It's not the same.

options.label: Guilt trip about timing
options.outcome: They stay an extra month out of guilt and hand over properly. They also tell everyone in the office exactly why they are really leaving.
options.failureOutcome: They walk that Friday, offended, with no handover at all. The story of the conversation spreads through the office ahead of you, and their files are a locked drawer nobody has the key to.

title: Office Illness
description: Something is going around the office. Three people called in sick today.

options.label: Redistribute workload
options.outcome: Those present pick up slack. Tiring but manageable.

options.label: Push back deadlines
options.outcome: You notify stakeholders of the delays. Most grumble and accept — everyone's office has a flu week eventually.
options.failureOutcome: One partner does not accept, because their referral window does not care about your flu week. The window closes, the relationship takes the real hit, and next week you are drafting an expedite request to recover ground you gave away by email.

options.label: Bring in temps
options.outcome: Agency staff fill the gap. Quality suffers but output continues.

title: Early Permit Approval
description: The ministry fast-tracked one of your applications. Approved ahead of schedule!

options.label: Celebrate with the team
options.outcome: You buy everyone coffee. Morale soars.

options.label: Use momentum to push others
options.outcome: You leverage the goodwill while it is warm. Two other applications move up the pile.
options.failureOutcome: You lean a call too hard and the contact bristles. The fast-track was a favour, not a precedent — your next file settles to the bottom of the pile, and you go back to waiting like everyone else.

options.label: Document what worked
options.outcome: You analyze why it went smoothly. Lessons for next time.

title: Partnership Opportunity
description: A First Nation partner offers to co-lead the referral process for their territory.

options.label: Accept enthusiastically
options.outcome: A collaborative approach begins. Slower but richer outcomes.

options.label: Accept with conditions
options.outcome: You set boundaries on scope and the Nation accepts them. The partnership starts carefully, on paper both sides can live with.
options.failureOutcome: The conditions read as distrust, and the offer is quietly withdrawn at the next council meeting. Consultation returns to the formal minimum — slower, colder, and now every referral goes through a Nation that remembers offering more.

options.label: Defer pending capacity review
options.outcome: You punt to later. Opportunity may not come again.

title: First Nations Consultation Phase
description: It is time to engage with local First Nations regarding upcoming harvest plans. How will you approach consultation?

options.label: Conduct comprehensive consultations with all Nations
options.outcome: Full consultations take time and money, but every Nation is heard and the plan is stronger for it.

options.label: Schedule individual meetings with each Nation
options.outcome: One-on-one meetings build real understanding, though a shared table might have surfaced more.

options.label: Send formal notification letters only (minimal compliance)
options.outcome: Letters go out and the legal box is ticked. Several Nations note, in writing, that a letter is not consultation.
options.partialOutcome: One Nation writes back asking for the meeting the letter should have offered. You schedule it under a cloud, and the minimal-compliance approach is now part of the meeting's agenda.
options.failureOutcome: A Nation formally challenges the adequacy of consultation, and the referral stalls under review. Every future file with that Nation now starts from documented distrust, and the harvest plan waits on a process you no longer control.

options.label: Delay consultations (risk deteriorating relationships)
options.outcome: The file goes quiet. Word gets around that consultation is being put off, and trust erodes a little more each week you do not call.
options.failureOutcome: A Nation forces the issue with a formal complaint to the district. The harvest plan freezes until consultation happens on their timeline, in their community, with your delay as the first item discussed.

title: Community Watershed Red Flag
description: A downstream intake concern lands on your desk. What looked like a routine road or block decision is now a sediment, timing, and trust problem.

options.label: Pause and co-write a mitigation plan
options.outcome: You slow the file down, walk the drainage with partners, and come back with a package people can actually defend.

options.label: Add stronger erosion controls and keep moving
options.outcome: The sharpened mitigation notes satisfy the intake owner, barely. The file stays alive and the water stays out of the news.
options.failureOutcome: The intake owner is not convinced by paper and escalates to the district. The file pauses anyway — now with the optics of having been pushed through — and the mitigation plan gets co-written after all, from a weaker seat.

options.label: Argue the risk is overstated
options.outcome: Your read of the drainage holds up and the schedule survives. Confidence in the file drops anyway, because arguing about drinking water always costs something.
options.partialOutcome: The district splits the difference: you keep moving under an attached monitoring condition. Someone now checks your sediment numbers monthly, and they did not pick the someone from your list.
options.failureOutcome: A hydrologist's rebuttal lands on the district's desk a week later and the file pauses on the spot. You are now the licensee who argued with the drinking-water file, and the mitigation plan you avoided gets written for you.

title: Caribou Timing Window Revision
description: Updated wildlife direction cuts into your planned access window. The block still works on paper, but not on the calendar you built around it.

options.label: Re-sequence the work to alternate ground
options.outcome: You protect the file by moving effort elsewhere, even if the quarter gets less efficient.

options.label: Request a monitored operating window
options.outcome: The biologists grant a narrow window under tighter conditions and much closer watch. The calendar survives, on their terms.
options.failureOutcome: Refused — and the request itself marks you as pushing on caribou. The window closes entirely, and you re-sequence to alternate ground anyway, three weeks later than if you had started the day the direction landed.

options.label: Push back on the revision
options.outcome: The district holds the line publicly but quietly lets your existing schedule stand. You keep the quarter and spend the capital.
options.failureOutcome: The pushback fails, in writing, and the direction comes back tighter than the draft. The capital is simply gone, the window is smaller than if you had said nothing, and the re-sequencing starts today.

title: Archaeology Screening Gap
description: Just before submission, the archaeology screening tells you the package needs stronger overview or permit context than the draft file carried.

options.label: Hold the file and bring in the right specialist
options.outcome: You lose time, but the package stops looking careless.

options.label: Revise maps and referral notes internally
options.outcome: The in-house patch holds. The package keeps moving, though everyone who touched it knows how thin the margin got.
options.failureOutcome: The archaeology branch spots the thin margin on the first pass and bounces the file with questions about who signed off. The specialist gets hired anyway — after the bounce, with your name now attached to the question.

options.label: Submit and hope the issue stays minor
options.outcome: The file leaves the office on time and clears screening without a second look. Nobody ever asks about the overview you did not strengthen.
options.partialOutcome: The reviewer asks for a supplementary overview before adjudication. The file waits while you produce, under deadline, exactly the work you skipped — and the request is on the record.
options.failureOutcome: Bounced, with a professional-reliance question attached to the referral response. The file and your name both go on a list, and everything you submit this year gets the long read.

title: Visual Quality Redraft
description: A sightline review catches your opening from town and the highway. The layout is efficient, but it is going to read hard on the landscape.

options.label: Re-shape the opening and soften the edge
options.outcome: The design gets better and the volume gets a little worse.

options.label: Add screening and phased harvesting notes
options.outcome: The reviewer accepts the notes as a serious answer. You keep most of the schedule and the sightline file closes quietly.
options.failureOutcome: Unpersuaded — the redraft is ordered anyway. You have now paid for the notes and the redesign, and the reviewer's memo suggests starting the reshape before the next referral cycle.

options.label: Defend the original shape
options.outcome: The reviewer files their concern and lets the layout stand. You save the office time and spend credibility doing it.
options.failureOutcome: The reviewer escalates and the redesign is ordered with a community-interface note attached to your file. You reshape the opening anyway — later, under direction, with the town watching.

title: FPBC Competence Audit
description: FPBC asks for your CPD record, competence declaration, professional development plan, and work samples tied to your current practice areas.

options.label: Clear the deck and submit a clean record
options.outcome: You slow the office down long enough to produce a defensible package. The audit feels thorough rather than hostile.

options.label: Bring in a mentor to tighten the file
options.outcome: A second set of eyes catches weak notes before the regulator does.

options.label: Send the minimum and move on
options.outcome: The regulator accepts the thin file without comment. Today's schedule survives, and the declaration goes in a drawer for another cycle.
options.partialOutcome: Accepted with comments: a professional development plan is now due in sixty days, and your name is flagged for the next audit cycle. The minimum bought you a deadline.
options.failureOutcome: The declaration is ruled insufficient and a formal competence review opens. It hangs over every file you sign this run, and clearing it means producing — under review — the record you declined to produce today.

title: Road Use Permit Gap
description: District staff point out your access plan needs a clearer Forest Service Road use permit and primary-user maintenance arrangement before the file can move cleanly.

options.label: Take the lead and formalize the maintenance split
options.outcome: It creates extra admin, but the district sees a credible access package.

options.label: Negotiate a user agreement first
options.outcome: A day of calls to the other industrial users lands a workable split. You bring the district a calmer road politics file than they asked for.
options.failureOutcome: One user stalls on cost-sharing and will not sign. The day is burned, the district is still waiting, and you end up formalizing the maintenance split yourself anyway — a week later, with the file marked as sitting.

options.label: Push traffic while the paperwork catches up
options.outcome: The paperwork catches up before anyone drives the road with a clipboard. The trucks never stopped, and the file closes as if it was always in order.
options.partialOutcome: A district tech logs your traffic on an unpermitted segment and a warning letter follows. The permit gets processed with conditions attached, and your hauling is now something the district watches.
options.failureOutcome: A stop-work order lands on the road and hauling halts mid-week. A compliance file opens with your name on the cover, and nothing moves until the permit — now unhurried — is issued.

title: Special Use Permit Bundle
description: The camp, helipad, and dump footprint are larger than expected, and the district now wants a proper special use permit package for the support sites.

options.label: Build the full permit bundle now
options.outcome: It is a paperwork-heavy week, but the support infrastructure stops undermining the main file.

options.label: Shrink the footprint and redraw the maps
options.outcome: You make operations less convenient but easier to authorize.

options.label: Use the sites quietly and hope nobody notices
options.outcome: The season ends before anyone flies over with a question. The camp comes out in October and the occupancy question never gets asked.
options.partialOutcome: An overflight photo of the helipad reaches the district. A retroactive application is ordered and filed at the back of the queue, and the support sites operate under sufferance while it waits.
options.failureOutcome: An unauthorized occupancy finding shuts the camp and helipad down mid-season. Crews demobilize while the permit bundle gets built anyway — under a compliance file, at demob prices.

title: Journalist Calls About Forestry Controversy
description: A journalist from a national outlet is on the phone. They have photos of a cutblock near a salmon-bearing creek and want your comment before the piece runs tonight.

options.label: No comment
options.outcome: The story runs with "declined to comment." Safe legally, but the public reads silence as guilt. Social media piles on.

options.label: Give a detailed on-the-record statement
options.outcome: You explain the science, the setbacks, the monitoring plan. The journalist keeps two careful sentences, and readers who look past the headline find the nuance.
options.partialOutcome: The piece runs with your quotes out of context, but the underlying numbers hold. You spend a day on follow-up letters and calls, and it ends roughly a wash.
options.failureOutcome: Your own quotes anchor a harder piece than silence would have earned. The ministry calls first thing, and the follow-up story is already being reported with you cast as the defensive licensee.

options.label: Redirect to PR department
options.outcome: PR sends a boilerplate response. The story is bland. Your ministry contact calls to ask why you didn't handle it yourself.

title: Competing Department Wants Your Budget
description: The Wildfire Division is arguing to the executive that your silviculture monitoring budget should be reallocated to their prevention program. They have a compelling case and political momentum.

options.label: Fight it with data and lobbying
options.outcome: Days of counter-cases and called-in favours keep most of your budget intact. The reserves of goodwill upstairs are what you spent instead.
options.failureOutcome: The executive sides with Wildfire anyway. The line item transfers, the favours are spent for nothing, and you replan the monitoring season around a hole — remembered as the manager who fought and lost.

options.label: Propose a compromise split
options.outcome: You offer 30% of the disputed line and both sides save face. The team does more with less and says so at every staff meeting.
options.failureOutcome: Wildfire pockets the 30% as an opening bid and comes back for the rest with momentum. You are now fighting the fight you tried to buy your way out of, from a weaker position and minus the down payment.

options.label: Concede gracefully
options.outcome: You give up the budget line with a public statement of support. The executive remembers your professionalism. Your work plan takes a hit.

title: Key Stakeholder Retirement
description: The regional biologist who has been your strongest ally for fifteen years just announced retirement. She knows every sensitive site, every handshake deal, every unwritten rule.

options.label: Host a farewell event
options.outcome: A proper send-off with speeches and gifts. She is moved — and before she leaves, her private notes on every sensitive file land on your desk.
options.failureOutcome: A lovely evening, warm speeches, and a firm handshake at the door. The notes were never hers to hand over, she decides, and fifteen years of unwritten rules retire with her — her replacement calls you with questions you cannot answer either.

options.label: Send a card and a gift
options.outcome: A nice gesture. She appreciates it. You get a polite email back and a promise to be available by phone. She mostly isn't.

options.label: Let it pass without ceremony
options.outcome: You're busy. She notices. When her replacement calls with questions, she doesn't suggest they reach out to you.

title: Whistleblower Allegation
description: An anonymous letter alleges that a contractor falsified replanting data on three cutblocks last season. The letter includes dates and block numbers that match your records.

options.label: Investigate thoroughly in-house
options.outcome: You pull files, walk the blocks, interview the contractor. Two of three allegations check out, you report honestly, and your integrity is on the record at the cost of a relationship.
options.failureOutcome: All three allegations check out, and worse, the pattern extends to a fourth block. The contractor is terminated mid-season, the region's replanting capacity goes with them, and your honest report now comes with a scramble to re-tender the work.

options.label: Quietly bury it
options.outcome: You file the letter where letters go to be forgotten, and nothing follows. The blocks stay signed off, the contractor keeps planting, and only you know the drawer it lives in.
options.partialOutcome: The whistleblower writes again — this time to your director, registered mail. You investigate after all, with the first letter's date sitting in the file, and every finding now doubles as evidence of the delay.
options.failureOutcome: Three months of quiet, then the allegations run in a provincial paper with a line about when your office first knew. The ministry's first question is not about the contractor, and the story you now manage is the burial, not the planting.

options.label: Forward to compliance division
options.outcome: You pass it up the chain with a cover memo. The investigation takes six months. Your name stays clean, but the contractor keeps working until findings are in.

title: Whistleblower Story Breaks in Media
description: The same allegations you received anonymously have now been published in a provincial newspaper. The article mentions that your office received the complaint months ago. The ministry is asking questions.

options.label: Come clean and launch an immediate investigation
options.outcome: You acknowledge the delay and throw resources at it. The damage is done but you stop the bleeding. Trust recovery will take a long time.

options.label: Claim the letter was under review
options.outcome: The half-truth holds. Most readers accept it, the journalist cannot prove otherwise, and the story cycles out without a follow-up.
options.failureOutcome: The journalist publishes the timeline, and the second story is about your office lying rather than the contractor cheating. The ministry stops returning calls, and you now answer for the cover story as well as the delay.

options.label: Resign from the file
options.outcome: You ask to be reassigned. It's an admission of failure but limits further damage to you personally. Your team is left holding the bag.

title: Audit Scheduled
description: A formal letter arrives: your district has been selected for a comprehensive compliance audit in three days. This time, it's not a surprise -- but the timeline is tight.

options.label: Drop everything and prepare
options.outcome: You pull the team off regular work for three days of file organization and documentation review. When the auditors arrive, you're ready.

options.label: Prepare what you can during normal hours
options.outcome: You do what you can without disrupting operations. Some gaps will be visible but nothing catastrophic.

options.label: Request a postponement
options.outcome: You cite operational pressures and they push it back two weeks. You are flagged as reluctant, but you have the time you asked for.
options.failureOutcome: Refused — the audit proceeds in three days as scheduled, and you spent one of them arguing about the date. The opening meeting begins with your postponement request on the table.

title: Auditor Arrives
description: The audit team is here. Three auditors, two days on-site. They want to see everything: permits, referral logs, consultation records, silviculture prescriptions.

options.label: Full transparency -- open the files
options.outcome: Unrestricted access turns up a few minor issues and a commendation for openness. The final report is fair, and it reads like it.
options.failureOutcome: In the open drawers they find a real gap — a referral closed without the sign-off it needed. The written finding is softened by your openness, but you now owe a remediation plan in thirty days and the gap has a name.

options.label: Guided tour -- show them what's ready
options.outcome: The strong files set the tone and the two days run out before the weak drawers come up. The report is clean, and only you know how the route was drawn.
options.partialOutcome: They notice the steering by the second morning. Pointed questions follow, and the report notes that access was 'facilitated' — a word that will be read carefully upstairs.
options.failureOutcome: The steering is read as concealment and written up as a systemic finding. The next audit will be unannounced, and the drawers you steered them past are now the first thing anyone opens.

options.label: Assign your weakest team member as liaison
options.outcome: They fumble questions and can't find documents. The auditors write it up as a systemic issue. You shouldn't have delegated this one.

title: First Nation Leadership Change
description: Election results are in: the First Nation community you work most closely with has a new Chief and Council. The previous Chief was a strong ally. The new one is an unknown quantity.

options.label: Request an introductory meeting immediately
options.outcome: You reach out within days. The new Chief appreciates the initiative but is guarded. A formal meeting is set.

options.label: Send a congratulatory letter and wait
options.outcome: A professional approach. The letter is acknowledged. Weeks pass before any substantive contact.

options.label: Continue business as usual
options.outcome: Operations proceed under the existing agreements while the new Council settles in. Nobody calls, which you choose to read as consent.
options.failureOutcome: The new Chief hears about the continuing operations from staff, not from you. Existing agreements are reopened for renegotiation, and your first meeting is now about why you never asked for one.

title: New Chief Requests Meeting
description: The new Chief arrives at your office with two councillors. They have a list of concerns about current operations, outstanding commitments, and a new vision for co-management.

options.label: Listen for the full session, take notes, commit to follow-up
options.outcome: Three hours later, you have a clear picture of their priorities. Some are costly. All are legitimate. A working relationship begins to form.

options.label: Present your existing plans and ask for their input
options.outcome: You show your work and they engage with it. The tone is professional but cool — consulted is not the same as heard, and everyone in the room knows it.
options.failureOutcome: Finished plans read as consultation theatre, and the meeting sours in the first half hour. A formal co-management demand lands the following week, and your plans are now the opening exhibit in that discussion.

options.label: Set firm boundaries on what's negotiable
options.outcome: You are honest about constraints and the Chief respects the candor. The meeting ends tense but with a real baseline neither side has to walk back.
options.failureOutcome: The boundaries read as bad faith on day one. Council takes the two contested items over your head to the ministry, and you spend next month defending positions you set in a first meeting.

title: Story Published About Your Operations
description: A story has been published about your operations. The angle depends on how past media inquiries were handled. Today's version focuses on old-growth harvesting near a community watershed.

options.label: Issue a detailed public rebuttal
options.outcome: The point-by-point response, with maps and data, holds. Professionals applaud, the public shrugs, and the story loses its legs.
options.failureOutcome: The rebuttal becomes the story: a second news cycle about the defensive licensee and their eleven-page response. You are now managing coverage of your reaction, and the original piece reads better every day.

options.label: Invite the journalist to a site tour
options.outcome: Bold move. They walk the ground, ask hard questions, and the follow-up piece is notably more balanced than the first.
options.partialOutcome: The follow-up is mostly fair, but the photo is a rutted skid trail with a careful caption. You spend a week answering letters about a picture instead of a practice.
options.failureOutcome: They find something on the tour you did not know was there to find. The second story is worse than the first and this time it has photos, and your own invitation is the first line of it.

options.label: Let it blow over
options.outcome: You don't respond. The story cycles out of the news in a week, but it lives on in Google searches forever.

title: Industry Award Nomination
description: Your district has been nominated for the Provincial Forestry Excellence Award for your consultation framework with First Nations. The ceremony is next month.

options.label: Accept and attend the ceremony
options.outcome: You and two team members attend. Win or lose, the recognition boosts team pride. The First Nation partners are pleased to be mentioned.

options.label: Accept but send a team member instead
options.outcome: Your senior analyst represents the district. She does well. The team notices you didn't go yourself.

options.label: Decline the nomination
options.outcome: You cite humility and the team's preference to keep their heads down. Some think you're being strategic. Others think you're foolish.

title: Mentor Offers Advice
description: Your former supervisor -- now retired -- calls out of the blue. She's heard about your challenges through the grapevine and offers to buy you lunch and talk things through.

options.label: Accept and take the full afternoon
options.outcome: Over two hours, she shares hard-won wisdom about navigating ministry politics, managing burnout, and picking your battles. You return to the office with clarity.

options.label: Accept but keep it short
options.outcome: A quick coffee. She gives you one key insight about a pending file that saves you a week of headaches.

options.label: Decline -- too busy right now
options.outcome: She understands. The offer probably won't come again in the same way. You handle things alone.

title: Team Celebrates Milestone
description: Your team just processed their 100th referral this fiscal year -- a district record. Someone brought in a cake. The mood is light for the first time in weeks.

options.label: Join the celebration and give a short speech
options.outcome: You acknowledge each person's contribution. Someone tears up. The team bonds. Afternoon productivity is zero but nobody cares.

options.label: Celebrate briefly and refocus on the backlog
options.outcome: You have cake, say congrats, then remind everyone about the 50 referrals still pending. The mood deflates slightly.

options.label: Skip it -- you have a meeting
options.outcome: You wave from your office doorway. The team celebrates without you. They notice.

title: Data Breach Scare
description: IT Security calls: a laptop with sensitive consultation records was left in a truck overnight. It might have been accessed. Encryption status is unclear.

options.label: Report immediately and notify affected parties
options.outcome: You file the breach report within the hour and call every affected Nation. The laptop turns out to be encrypted — the panic was unnecessary, and the speed of your call is what everyone remembers.
options.failureOutcome: The laptop was not encrypted. It is a real breach: formal notifications, consultation records in the wind, and months of rebuilding trust with Nations whose information your truck lost — though nobody can fault the reporting.

options.label: Investigate quietly before reporting
options.outcome: IT confirms the encryption inside the hour and the report goes in clean. Nobody ever asks about the gap in the timestamps.
options.partialOutcome: Encrypted — no breach. But the four-hour gap between discovery and report gets its own line in the incident file, and mandatory reporting is not graded on outcomes.
options.failureOutcome: Not encrypted, and you sat on it for four hours. The delayed report becomes its own compliance file alongside the breach, and every notification call now starts with an apology for the timing.

options.label: Have IT wipe the laptop remotely
options.outcome: The data is destroyed. Problem solved -- except you just wiped active case files. Two weeks of work is gone.

title: Contractor Billing Dispute
description: Your primary silviculture contractor submitted an invoice $18,000 over the agreed contract price. They claim extra work was verbally authorized by a field supervisor. Your supervisor doesn't remember it that way.

options.label: Pay the full amount to preserve the relationship
options.outcome: You process the invoice. The contractor is happy. Finance flags it in their quarterly review. Your budget takes the hit.

options.label: Negotiate a compromise
options.outcome: Two tense meetings end at half. Both sides feel they gave up too much, which is roughly what a fair settlement feels like.
options.failureOutcome: Talks collapse on the second meeting and they lawyer up mid-season. Nothing gets planted while it is in dispute, and you are now managing a legal file and an idle silviculture program at the same time.

options.label: Reject the overage and cite the contract
options.outcome: You send a firm letter. The contractor is furious but finishes current obligations — and will never again do extras on a handshake, which was rather the point.
options.failureOutcome: They walk off current obligations and file a claim for the full amount. The season's silviculture is suddenly uncrewed in a region with a short contractor list, and your firm letter is now exhibit A.

title: Wildfire Approaching Operations Area
description: Fire weather is extreme. A wildfire 30 km from your active cutblock is growing. Evacuation hasn't been ordered yet, but the wind forecast is bad.

options.label: Preemptively shut down operations and evacuate
options.outcome: You pull everyone out a day before the order comes. The fire turns and misses the block — the call was right, and people will still question it at budget time.
options.failureOutcome: The fire takes the block two days later: roads, culverts, and standing timber. The evacuation call is fully vindicated, and you now replan the season around burned ground instead of harvest schedules.

options.label: Continue with enhanced monitoring
options.outcome: You double the fire watch and keep working. The wind holds, the evacuation never comes, and you got away with betting a crew on a forecast.
options.failureOutcome: The wind shifts mid-shift and the evacuation is a scramble, with equipment abandoned behind the fire line. Everyone gets out, WorkSafe wants the decision log, and the crew remembers exactly who kept them on the block.

options.label: Request official guidance from the ministry
options.outcome: By the time the guidance comes, you've lost a full day waiting. The recommendation is to continue with caution. Bureaucracy at its finest.

title: Professional Development Opportunity
description: A three-day Indigenous consultation training workshop is being offered next month. It's highly regarded but expensive, and you'd need to send at least two people to make it worthwhile.

options.label: Send two team members and attend yourself
options.outcome: Three of you spend three days learning. The team brings back concrete improvements to consultation processes. Operations slow while you're away.

options.label: Send two junior staff members
options.outcome: Good development opportunity for them. They return energized with new ideas, some practical, some less so.

options.label: Pass on it this year
options.outcome: Budget preserved. Your team's consultation skills remain where they are. The district next door sends four people and won't stop talking about it.

title: Interagency Jurisdiction Dispute
description: The provincial environmental assessment office claims your latest referral should have gone through their process, not yours. They're cc'ing the Deputy Minister.

options.label: Concede jurisdiction and hand over the file
options.outcome: You give up the file. It will take them six months to process what you could have done in six weeks. But it's technically their call.

options.label: Push back with a legal interpretation
options.outcome: The ADM backs your reading of the legislation. The file stays yours, jurisdiction is settled in writing, and the weeks of meetings were the price of the precedent.
options.partialOutcome: The ADM splits the difference: you keep this file, and a joint-review protocol applies to everything after it. You won the battle and standardized the war.
options.failureOutcome: The ADM sides with the assessment office. The file transfers anyway after weeks of meetings, and your branch wears the fight it started — the next jurisdictional grey area will not be given the benefit of the doubt.

options.label: Propose joint processing
options.outcome: Both offices contribute and the file lands, slower than either process alone but with a precedent for collaboration attached. The Deputy Minister's office notices the absence of a fight.
options.failureOutcome: The other office plays at half speed and the file enters dual-office limbo, slower than either process and owned by neither. Both sides blame you for the precedent, and you end up asking the ADM to untangle what you proposed.

title: Elder Offers Traditional Knowledge
description: A respected Elder from a partner Nation offers to share traditional ecological knowledge about a watershed you're planning to log. This information isn't in any database. She wants assurances about how it will be used.

options.label: Accept with a formal data-sharing agreement
options.outcome: You work with the Nation's governance team to draft an agreement. It takes three weeks but the knowledge shared changes your harvest plan fundamentally. Two culturally significant sites are protected.

options.label: Accept informally with verbal assurances
options.outcome: She shares some of what she knows — helpful but incomplete, because informality has limits she understands better than you do. You adjust the plan where you can.
options.failureOutcome: Something she shared informally surfaces in a referral document six weeks later. The Nation sees a broken assurance, consultation turns adversarial, and the formal agreement you skipped gets negotiated anyway — from distrust.

options.label: Decline -- regulatory process doesn't require it
options.outcome: Technically true. The Elder is deeply offended. Word spreads. Future consultation with this Nation becomes adversarial.

title: Critical Equipment Failure
description: The large-format plotter that prints your operational maps just died. Repair estimate: two weeks. A replacement would be faster but costs $12,000. You have permit submissions due in four days.

options.label: Buy a replacement immediately
options.outcome: New plotter arrives in two days. Maps printed, permits submitted on time. Finance asks pointed questions about unbudgeted capital purchases.

options.label: Use a print shop in town
options.outcome: You send files to the local print shop. Quality is acceptable but not great. Cost is moderate. You lose a day to file formatting issues.

options.label: Submit digital-only and request accommodation
options.outcome: The ministry accepts digital maps, reluctantly, and notes the precedent they did not want to set. The permits go in on time.
options.failureOutcome: Refused — hard copies or nothing. You are now four days from deadline with no plotter, paying the print shop rush rate anyway, and the permits go in late with the delay marked in your file.

title: Anonymous Tip About Poaching
description: A note slipped under your door reports illegal hunting in one of your active cutblocks. The description matches a vehicle belonging to a contractor's crew member.

options.label: Report to Conservation Officer Service
options.outcome: You pass it along with the details. COS investigates. The contractor is furious that you didn't come to them first. The crew member is charged.

options.label: Confront the contractor directly
options.outcome: You raise it privately and the contractor fires the crew member the same day. Solved, appreciated, and documented nowhere.
options.failureOutcome: The contractor denies everything and closes ranks, and the activity continues. When COS eventually gets its own tip, the file shows your office knew first and went nowhere official — and now you answer for the gap.

options.label: Increase site monitoring but take no direct action
options.outcome: You add patrols and the activity stops. You will never know if the tip was accurate, and the note-leaver clearly expected more.
options.failureOutcome: The poaching continues until a kill site is found by hikers, and it is public within the week. The paper trail shows you were tipped and did nothing formal, and COS now conducts its investigation through your office rather than with it.

title: Contractor Demands Meeting After Investigation
description: The contractor whose crew member was charged is at your office door. He's angry. He says your report cost him a good worker and damaged his reputation. He wants to know why you didn't call him first.

options.label: Explain your legal obligations calmly
options.outcome: You walk through the reporting requirements. He doesn't like it but understands. The professional relationship survives, barely.

options.label: Apologize for the process and offer future courtesy
options.outcome: You promise to give him a heads-up in the future before reporting. It's a promise that could come back to bite you.

options.label: Stand firm and end the conversation
options.outcome: You tell him you would do the same thing again. He storms out, and his next bid arrives 30% higher — but it arrives.
options.failureOutcome: He is done — no bid next season, and he says so to every operator he drinks with. The regional contractor pool just got smaller, and your next tender comes back with one envelope in it.

title: Unexpected Grant Opportunity
description: A federal climate adaptation fund just opened applications. Your riparian restoration project is a perfect fit. Deadline is in five days.

options.label: Drop everything and write the application
options.outcome: You and your best writer spend three days on a strong submission, and it is funded — $45,000 in new money for riparian work. The regular files waited and it was worth it.
options.failureOutcome: A strong submission, reviewed and not funded — the panel liked another district's watershed more. Three days are gone, the backlog grew, and the riparian project goes back on the someday list you took it from.

options.label: Submit a quick application with existing materials
options.outcome: Against the odds, the panel funds a scaled version — $12,000 for the highest-priority reach. Sometimes lightning strikes a two-hour application.
options.partialOutcome: Reviewed and declined with a polite form letter, as cobbled applications usually are. Two hours gone, nothing more.
options.failureOutcome: Declined — and the program officer remembers the district that submitted recycled boilerplate. Next intake, your applications start from a deficit you wrote yourself.

options.label: Pass -- can't afford the time right now
options.outcome: The money goes to another district. Your riparian project stays unfunded. Sometimes the right call still feels wrong.

title: Surprise Office Renovation
description: Facilities just announced they're replacing the HVAC system. Your floor will be without climate control for a week. It's July. Temperatures are forecast to hit 35 degrees.

options.label: Set up temporary workspace in the field office
options.outcome: You relocate the team to the cramped field office. Internet is slow, printer doesn't work, but you're functional and cool.

options.label: Allow remote work for the week
options.outcome: Everyone works from home and, on balance, it works. The referral queue moves, and the team remembers being trusted.
options.failureOutcome: Half the office is unreachable by Wednesday, and a referral misses its response window during the week nobody was there. You spend the following Monday apologizing to a partner agency about your HVAC.

options.label: Buy portable AC units and power through
options.outcome: You buy three units on a corporate card. The office is tolerable. The noise makes phone calls impossible. Finance adds it to your ledger.

title: Species at Risk Discovered
description: A biologist conducting pre-harvest surveys found a northern goshawk nest in a cutblock scheduled for harvest next month. This triggers federal species-at-risk protections. The harvest plan, contractor mobilization, and timber sale revenue are all at stake.

options.label: Halt the harvest and redesign the block
options.outcome: You pull the block from the schedule, establish a buffer zone, and redesign. The right thing ecologically. The timber sale volume drops by 15%. The contractor idles equipment for two weeks at your cost.

options.label: Apply for an exception permit
options.outcome: Two months later the exception is granted with conditions: a reduced footprint under monitoring. Rare, defensible, and on the record as done properly.
options.partialOutcome: The decision comes back 'insufficient information — resubmission invited.' A month is gone, the nest is still there, and you now face the same halt-or-apply choice with less season left to spend on it.
options.failureOutcome: Denied after two months of waiting. The season is gone, and you spent it holding a contractor on standby instead of redesigning the block — which is where you now start, in the fall.

options.label: Verify the identification before acting
options.outcome: You send a second biologist. The ID is confirmed. You've lost three days but now have bulletproof documentation for whatever you decide next.

title: Intern Produces Outstanding Analysis
description: Your summer intern, working on a side project, has produced a spatial analysis that identifies $200,000 in potential cost savings across your road maintenance program. The analysis is solid. The presentation needs work.

options.label: Present it to senior management with the intern
options.outcome: She is nervous and impressive in the same ten minutes. The savings are real, the district looks innovative, and she leaves the room with a job offer.
options.failureOutcome: She freezes on the second question and the methodology gets picked apart live. The savings are shelved pending revalidation, and you re-pitch the same numbers next budget season without the shine.

options.label: Present it yourself and credit the intern
options.outcome: You polish the presentation and deliver it. You mention the intern's contribution. Some credit flows down. Most flows to you.

options.label: Sit on it until the methodology is bulletproof
options.outcome: You ask for more validation. By the time it's ready, budget season is over. The savings are implemented next year. The intern's contract has ended.

title: Cross-Cultural Miscommunication
description: A field crew inadvertently cleared brush from an area that a First Nation identifies as a ceremonial site. It wasn't marked on any maps. The community is upset. The damage is mostly to understory vegetation -- recoverable, but symbolically significant.

options.label: Personally visit the community to apologize
options.outcome: You drive three hours, sit with the Chief and Elders, listen, and apologize without excuses. They appreciate the sincerity. A restoration plan is agreed to. The relationship heals slowly.

options.label: Send a formal letter of apology with a restoration offer
options.outcome: The letter is well written and the restoration offer is real. The community acknowledges it — paper is not presence, but the file stays workable.
options.failureOutcome: A letter, for a ceremonial site, reads as distance — and the community says so publicly. Consultation on your other files chills, and you end up making the three-hour drive anyway, weeks later, to a much colder room.

options.label: Point out the site wasn't mapped and offer to map it now
options.outcome: Technically accurate. Relationally catastrophic. The community sees it as blaming them for your crew's actions. Consultation on three other projects is now in jeopardy.

title: Board Chair Wants the Numbers Early
description: The board chair calls at 7:40 a.m. He is golfing with two institutional investors on Thursday and would like the quarterly numbers 'directionally, nothing fancy' -- which means a full pack, footnoted, by Wednesday.

options.label: Build the pack properly
options.outcome: Finance loses two evenings, but every figure survives contact with the investors. The chair takes the credit. That's the job.

options.label: Send topline numbers with caveats in bold
options.outcome: The chair reads the bold print, repeats nothing he should not, and the golf goes fine. Finance keeps its evenings and you bank a small favour.
options.failureOutcome: A bare number circulates among the investors without its footnote, and by Friday it has compounded. You spend the day walking it back caller by caller, and the audited pack will now be read against the version from the back nine.

options.label: Suggest the numbers wait for the audited pack
options.outcome: Prudent, defensible, and exactly the kind of answer that gets you described as 'not commercial' in board washrooms.

title: Activist Shareholder Letter
description: A Vancouver fund holding four percent of the company writes to ask why your cost per cubic metre runs above the coast average, and whether the answer involves 'legacy attitudes.' They have cc'd the board.

options.label: Open the books and host a site tour
options.outcome: They arrive in brand-new caulk boots and leave impressed despite themselves. The follow-up letter is almost warm.
options.failureOutcome: In the open books they find their own story — a cost line you had explanations for but no appetite to defend in public. The follow-up letter quotes your numbers back at the board, and the next quarter's pack gets built to answer it.

options.label: Have legal draft a courteous nothing
options.outcome: Three pages that commit to no figure and no date. The fund reads it for what it is and starts phoning your directors individually.

options.label: Rebut with your own benchmarking
options.outcome: Your numbers are decent enough to hold, and the fund moves on to a softer target. The exchange costs some polish and nothing structural.
options.failureOutcome: The fund escalates to a public campaign with the board cc'd, and the stalemate becomes a governance story in the trade press. You are now preparing AGM materials around a fight your covering letter started.

title: Woodlands and Silviculture Stop Talking
description: Your woodlands manager and silviculture superintendent now communicate exclusively through forwarded emails with the subject line 'per my last.' Planting windows are at stake, and so is the lunchroom seating plan.

options.label: Lock them in a room with a map and no chairs
options.outcome: Forty minutes standing over the divisional map produces a schedule both sides claim they suggested. Peace, of a kind.
options.failureOutcome: The standoff hardens with an audience, and one of them files a formal grievance about the meeting itself. The planting window slips while HR mediates, and the schedule you needed gets written by a facilitator.

options.label: Side with woodlands -- the wood pays the bills
options.outcome: The schedule favours harvest. Silviculture plants late into the hot window and quietly starts documenting everything.

options.label: Let them sort it out like adults
options.outcome: They do not sort it out like adults. A seedling order misses its lift date, and the cold-storage invoice finds your desk anyway.

title: A Competitor Courts Your CEO
description: An Alberta outfit with deeper pockets and shallower cutblocks has taken your CEO to dinner twice this month. Your executive assistant noticed the second reservation was for the good steakhouse.

options.label: Counter with money and a longer leash
options.outcome: The retention package stings, but the CEO stays — and now knows exactly what staying is worth.
options.failureOutcome: Your counter becomes their floor in Alberta, and they leave anyway with a better number than the steakhouse offered. You have published what the job is worth, and the search firm quotes you your own figure.

options.label: Appeal to the work, not the wallet
options.outcome: You talk tenure, stewardship, and finishing what was started. It lands — this time — and the steakhouse will still be there next quarter.
options.failureOutcome: The dinners were further along than you knew, and the resignation letter arrives inside the month. The succession scramble is cold and public, and the board asks why there was no retention offer on the table.

options.label: Quietly start shortlisting successors
options.outcome: Word gets out that you're shopping, because word always gets out. The CEO's lawyer calls your lawyer. Productive quarter all around.

title: Certification Surveillance Audit Booked
description: The certification body has booked its annual surveillance audit for the week after next. The lead auditor is the one who once wrote up a licensee for a coffee cup left in a riparian zone.

options.label: Run a full internal pre-audit
options.outcome: Two findings surface in-house, which means they get fixed instead of cited. The audit closes with zero non-conformities and one approving remark about your record-keeping.

options.label: Tidy what the auditor will actually see
options.outcome: She walks the spotless route, reads the clean files, and closes out with a remark about good housekeeping. The rest of the operation stays as it was, unexamined.
options.partialOutcome: One minor non-conformity surfaces in a place you did not expect her to look — because she has read this play before. The finding is small; the note about where she found it is not.
options.failureOutcome: She recognizes the staging and writes up the staging itself: a major non-conformity for management-system integrity. Certification is suspended pending re-audit, and the quarter now belongs to proving the system is real.

options.label: Trust the system you already run
options.outcome: The audit lands one minor and one observation. Your certification survives, and your operations forester ages a year in a week.
options.failureOutcome: The system has a hole nobody knew about, and once she finds it the findings compound. Recertification becomes the quarter's project, with a corrective-action plan due before the next surveillance visit.
